content.thinking:
This peer-review intervention frames scientific scrutiny as a rigorous test that competitors would gladly expose flaws in, which builds credibility through integrity and accountability rather than pure authority. It's fairly dry but effective, and its consensus framing might also nudge belief slightly — I'd put trust_multidimensional around +2.2 and trust_post near +1.6.

Working through the remaining diluted metrics — distrust_post, funding_perceptions, policy_role, institutional trust, belief, concern, policy attitudes, and behavior — the peer-review arm lands as a solid mid-to-upper trust performer since it directly targets integrity and accountability, so I'll settle trust_multidimensional at roughly +2.3.

It is didactic rather than narrative and has no messenger congruence or interactive correction, so I place it slightly above the average trust arm but below vivid source-credibility/messenger or misinformation-exposure arms: ~+2.3 on the fresh trust battery, shrunk to ~+1.6 on the pre-anchored single trust item and about -1.2 on distrust (asymmetric because distrust items are stickier and skew low). Downstream outcomes get progressively smaller effects since the text says nothing about funding, scientists' policy role, or personal action: belief gets a modest consensus-mediated bump (~+1), concern and general policy ~+0.5, specific policies and behavioral intentions under half a point. Institutional trust is diluted by the federal-government item, so ~+0.9 despite peer review being a university/journal-linked process. parsed_output.reasoning_summary: The peer-review text is a procedural-credibility (epistemic quality-control) message: it argues that climate findings survive adversarial scrutiny by competing independent experts, directly targeting the integrity, competence and openness dimensions of the multidimensional trust battery, with a secondary consensus cue ('experts from across the world consistently reach the same conclusions'). It is didactic rather than narrative and has no messenger congruence or interactive correction, so I place it slightly above the average trust arm but below vivid source-credibility/messenger or misinformation-exposure arms: ~+2.3 on the fresh trust battery, shrunk to ~+1.6 on the pre-anchored single trust item and about -1.2 on distrust (asymmetric because distrust items are stickier and skew low). Downstream outcomes get progressively smaller effects since the text says nothing about funding, scientists' policy role, or personal action: belief gets a modest consensus-mediated bump (~+1), concern and general policy ~+0.5, specific policies and behavioral intentions under half a point. Institutional trust is diluted by the federal-government item, so ~+0.9 despite peer review being a university/journal-linked process. Incentivized outcomes stay near zero: a few cents on the AMS donation and under one percentage point on newsletter sign-up, consistent with megastudy evidence that attitude shifts rarely translate into costly behavior.
